prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points on the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point in the plane such that the lines $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.
answer: Proof: $X$, $Y$ are the reflections of the incircle touch points in the midpoints of $AB$, $AC$, so the circumcentre $O$ is the midpoint of $IP$. Since $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac A2>2A=\angle BOC$, $I$ is inside circle $BOC$, so $P$ is outside it (on $A$'s side of $BC$) and $\angle BPC<\angle BOC=2A<120^\circ$.

solutions.title: The circumcentre is the midpoint of $IP$
solutions.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, let $I$ be the incentre and $D$, $E$ the points where the incircle touches $AB$, $AC$; let $O$ be the circumcentre and $M_c$, $M_b$ the midpoints of $AB$, $AC$.

**Locating $X$ and $Y$.** From $b+AX=a+BX$ and $AX+BX=c$ we get $AX=\frac{a+c-b}2$. The tangent lengths give $BD=\frac{a+c-b}2$. So $AX=BD$: on line $AB$, $X$ is the reflection of $D$ in the midpoint $M_c$. Similarly $AY=\frac{a+b-c}2=CE$, so $Y$ is the reflection of $E$ in $M_b$.

**$O$ is the midpoint of $IP$.** Let $Q$ be the midpoint of $IP$. Orthogonal projection onto a line is an affine map, so the projection of $Q$ onto $AB$ is the midpoint of the projections of $I$ and $P$, namely of $D$ and $X$, which is $M_c$. Likewise the projection of $Q$ onto $AC$ is the midpoint of $E$ and $Y$, which is $M_b$. So $Q$ lies on the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$, i.e. $Q=O$. Hence $P=2O-I$ (as vectors).

**Comparing angles.** Since $\angle A<60^\circ<90^\circ$, $O$ lies on the same side of $BC$ as $A$ and $\angle BOC=2\angle A$. Also $\angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{\angle A}2$. As $\angle A<60^\circ$, $2\angle A<90^\circ+\frac{\angle A}2$, i.e. $\angle BIC>\angle BOC$.

Let $\omega$ be the circle through $B$, $O$, $C$. For points $Z$ on the same side of $BC$ as $O$, $\angle BZC$ is larger than, equal to, or smaller than $\angle BOC$ according as $Z$ is inside, on, or outside $\omega$. Since $I$ is on that side (inside the triangle) and $\angle BIC>\angle BOC$, $I$ is strictly inside $\omega$.

The point $P$ lies on ray $IO$ beyond $O$ (with $OP=IO$). The line $IO$ meets $\omega$ in $O$ and in one more point, and $I$, being inside, lies between them; so the points of the ray from $I$ through $O$ that lie beyond $O$ are outside $\omega$. Hence $P$ is outside $\omega$.

$P$ is on the same side of $BC$ as $A$: signed distances to line $BC$ are affine, so $d(P)=2d(O)-d(I)=2R\cos A-r$, where $R$, $r$ are the circumradius and inradius. Since $\cos A>\frac12$, $2R\cos A>R>r$ (the incircle lies inside the triangle, hence inside the circumcircle, so $r<R$). Thus $d(P)>0$.

Therefore $\angle BPC<\angle BOC=2\angle A<120^\circ$. ∎

prompt: Students in a class form groups each of which contains exactly three members such that any two distinct groups have at most one member in common. Prove that, when the class size is $46$, there is a set of $10$ students in which no group is properly contained.
answer: Proof: take a largest set $S$ containing no whole group; if $|S|\le9$, every outsider $v$ forms a group with two members of $S$, different outsiders use different pairs, but there are $\ge37$ outsiders and only $\binom92=36$ pairs.

solutions.title: A maximal group-free set
solutions.body:
("No group is contained in the set" means no group has all three members in it.) Call a set of students *free* if it contains no group. The empty set is free; let $S$ be a free set of maximum size $s$. If $s\ge10$, any $10$ students of $S$ form a free set and we are done. Suppose $s\le9$.

Take any student $v\notin S$. By maximality $S\cup\{v\}$ is not free, so it contains a group; this group is not inside $S$, so it is $\{v,x,y\}$ with $x,y\in S$. Assign to $v$ such a pair $\{x,y\}$.

Different outsiders get different pairs: if $v\ne w$ were both assigned $\{x,y\}$, the distinct groups $\{v,x,y\}$ and $\{w,x,y\}$ would share two members.

So the number of students outside $S$ is at most the number of pairs in $S$:
$$46-s\le\binom s2\le\binom92=36 .$$
But $46-s\ge37$ — a contradiction. Hence $s\ge10$, and there is a set of $10$ students containing no group. ∎

prompt: Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$. A circle passing through points $A$ and $C$ meets the sides $BC$ and $BA$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. The lines $AD$ and $CE$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $G$ and $H$, respectively. The tangent lines of $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $C$ meet the line $DE$ at $L$ and $M$, respectively. Prove that the lines $LH$ and $MG$ meet at $\Gamma$.
answer: Proof: $MC=MD$, so $MD^2=MG\cdot MP$ for the second intersection $P$ of $MG$ with $\Gamma$; hence $MD$ is tangent to circle $DGP$ and an angle chase puts $P$ on circle $BDE$. Likewise the second intersection of $LH$ with $\Gamma$ lies on circle $BDE$, so both lines pass through the second common point of $\Gamma$ and circle $BDE$.

solutions.title: Both lines pass through the second intersection of $\Gamma$ and circle $BDE$
solutions.body:
We use directed angles between lines, $\angle(\ell,m)$, taken mod $180^\circ$. Let $\omega$ be the circle through $A,C,D,E$ and $\Gamma'$ the circle through $B,D,E$. $D$ and $E$ are interior points of the sides, so they lie inside $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'\ne\Gamma$.

**Step 1: $MC=MD$.** By the tangent–chord angle, $\angle(CM,CD)=\angle(CM,CB)=\angle(AC,AB)$. Since $A,C,D,E$ are concyclic, $\angle(DM,DC)=\angle(DE,DC)=\angle(AE,AC)=\angle(AB,AC)$. Hence $\angle(CM,CD)=-\angle(DM,DC)=\angle(DC,DM)$: triangle $MCD$ has equal base angles at $C$ and $D$, so $MC=MD$.

**Step 2.** $M\ne C$ lies on the tangent at $C$, so it is outside $\Gamma$. Let $P$ be the second intersection of line $MG$ with $\Gamma$. By the power of $M$,
$$MD^2=MC^2=MG\cdot MP .$$
Hence line $MD$ is tangent at $D$ to the circle through $D,G,P$ (converse of the power of a point; if $P=G$ the line $MG$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ and the computation below works with $GP$ read as that tangent). The tangent–chord angle in circle $DGP$ and then the inscribed angles in $\Gamma$ give
$$\angle(DE,DP)=\angle(DM,DP)=\angle(GD,GP)=\angle(GA,GP)=\angle(BA,BP)=\angle(BE,BP).$$
So, if $P\ne B$, the points $B,E,D,P$ are concyclic: **$P\in\Gamma'$.**

If $P=B$, the first three equalities still give $\angle(DE,DB)=\angle(GA,GB)$. Let $t$, $t'$ be the tangents at $B$ to $\Gamma$ and to $\Gamma'$. By the tangent–chord angle, $\angle(t,BA)=\angle(GB,GA)$ in $\Gamma$ and $\angle(t',BE)=\angle(DB,DE)$ in $\Gamma'$. Hence
$$\angle(t',BA)=\angle(DB,DE)=-\angle(DE,DB)=-\angle(GA,GB)=\angle(GB,GA)=\angle(t,BA),$$
so $t'=t$: **$\Gamma'$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $B$.**

**Step 3.** The configuration is symmetric under $A\leftrightarrow C$, $D\leftrightarrow E$, $G\leftrightarrow H$, $L\leftrightarrow M$ (circle $\Gamma'$ is unchanged). So the second intersection $Q$ of line $LH$ with $\Gamma$ satisfies: $Q\in\Gamma'$ if $Q\ne B$, and $\Gamma'$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ at $B$ if $Q=B$.

**Conclusion.** The circles $\Gamma\ne\Gamma'$ share the point $B$.
- If they are tangent at $B$, then $B$ is their only common point, so $P=Q=B$.
- If not, they meet at $B$ and exactly one further point $X$. Then $P\ne B$ and $Q\ne B$ (either equality would force tangency), so $P,Q\in\Gamma\cap\Gamma'\setminus\{B\}=\{X\}$, i.e. $P=Q=X$.

In both cases the lines $MG$ and $LH$ pass through the same point $P=Q$ of $\Gamma$. ∎

prompt:
Consider the function $f : \mathbb{N}_0 \to \mathbb{N}_0$, where $\mathbb{N}_0$ is the set of all non-negative integers, defined by the following conditions:

(i) $f(0) = 0$, (ii) $f(2n) = 2f(n)$ and (iii) $f(2n + 1) = n + 2f(n)$ for all $n \ge 0$.

(a) Determine the three sets $L := \{ n \mid f(n) < f(n + 1) \}$, $E := \{ n \mid f(n) = f(n + 1) \}$, and $G := \{ n \mid f(n) > f(n + 1) \}$.

(b) For each $k \ge 0$, find a formula for $a_k := \max\{f(n) : 0 \le n \le 2^k\}$ in terms of $k$.

solutions.title: Parity cases and a growth lemma
solutions.body:
**(a)** The three candidate sets $\{2k:k\ge1\}$, $\{0\}\cup\{4k+1\}$, $\{4k+3\}$ partition $\mathbb N_0$, and $L,E,G$ are disjoint, so it suffices to show each candidate lies in the corresponding set.

- $n=2k$, $k\ge1$: $f(2k+1)-f(2k)=k>0$, so $n\in L$. For $n=0$: $f(1)=0=f(0)$, so $0\in E$.
- $n=4k+1$: $f(4k+1)=2k+2f(2k)=2k+4f(k)$ and $f(4k+2)=2f(2k+1)=2k+4f(k)$; equal, so $n\in E$.
- $n=4k+3$: first a **lemma**: $f(m+1)-f(m)\le m$ for all $m\ge0$. By strong induction: for $m=2t$ the difference is $t\le m$; for $m=2t+1$,
$$f(2t+2)-f(2t+1)=2f(t+1)-t-2f(t)=2\big(f(t+1)-f(t)\big)-t\le2t-t=t\le m,$$
using the induction hypothesis for $t<m$. Now
$$f(4k+4)-f(4k+3)=4f(k+1)-\big(2k+1+2f(2k+1)\big)=4f(k+1)-(4k+1+4f(k))=4\big(f(k+1)-f(k)\big)-(4k+1)\le4k-4k-1<0,$$
so $n\in G$.

**Answer (a):** $L=\{n>0: n\text{ even}\}$, $E=\{0\}\cup\{n: n\equiv1\pmod 4\}$, $G=\{n:n\equiv3\pmod4\}$.

**(b)** Let $b_k=f(2^k-1)$. Since $2^k-1=2(2^{k-1}-1)+1$, rule (iii) gives
$$b_k=2b_{k-1}+2^{k-1}-1\quad(k\ge1),\qquad b_0=f(0)=0 .$$
Dividing by $2^k$: $\frac{b_k}{2^k}=\frac{b_{k-1}}{2^{k-1}}+\frac12-\frac1{2^k}$, so $\frac{b_k}{2^k}=\frac k2-\left(1-\frac1{2^k}\right)$, i.e.
$$b_k=k\,2^{k-1}-2^k+1 .$$
**Claim:** $a_k=b_k$ for all $k\ge0$. For $k=0$: $a_0=\max(f(0),f(1))=0=b_0$. Assume $a_{k-1}=b_{k-1}$ and let $0\le n\le2^k$.
- $n=2t$: then $t\le2^{k-1}$, and $f(n)=2f(t)\le2b_{k-1}\le b_k$ (as $2^{k-1}-1\ge0$).
- $n=2t+1\le2^k-1$: then $t\le2^{k-1}-1$, and $f(n)=t+2f(t)\le2^{k-1}-1+2b_{k-1}=b_k$.

So $f(n)\le b_k$ on $[0,2^k]$, with equality at $n=2^k-1$; hence $a_k=b_k$.

**Answer (b):** $a_k=k\,2^{k-1}-2^k+1$ (e.g. $a_2=1$, $a_3=5$, $a_4=17$).

prompt: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be integers satisfying $0 < a < c - 1$ and $1 < b < c$. For each $k$, $0 \le k \le a$, let $r_k$, $0 \le r_k < c$, be the remainder of $kb$ when divided by $c$. Prove that the two sets $\{r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_a\}$ and $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, a\}$ are different.
answer: Proof: if they were equal, $\sum_{k=0}^a x^{kb}\equiv\sum_{j=0}^a x^j \pmod{x^c-1}$; multiplying by $(x-1)(x^b-1)$ gives $x^{ab+b+1}+x^b+x^{a+1}\equiv x^{ab+b}+x^{a+b+1}+x$, so $b$ is congruent mod $c$ to $ab+b$, $a+b+1$ or $1$ — each impossible.

solutions.title: Generating polynomials modulo $x^c-1$
solutions.body:
Suppose the two sets are equal. Since $\{0,\dots,a\}$ has $a+1$ elements, the remainders $r_0,\dots,r_a$ are distinct and are a permutation of $0,1,\dots,a$. As $a\ge1$, some $r_k=1$, i.e. $kb\equiv1\pmod c$; hence $\gcd(b,c)=1$.

Work with polynomials modulo $x^c-1$. If $m\equiv m'\pmod c$, say $m=m'+cq$ with $q\ge0$, then $x^{m}-x^{m'}=x^{m'}(x^{cq}-1)$ is divisible by $x^c-1$. Hence $x^{kb}\equiv x^{r_k}$, and since the $r_k$ are a permutation of $0,\dots,a$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{a}x^{kb}\equiv\sum_{j=0}^{a}x^{j}\pmod{x^c-1}.$$
Multiply by $(x-1)(x^b-1)$ and use $\sum_{k=0}^a x^{kb}=\frac{x^{(a+1)b}-1}{x^b-1}$, $\sum_{j=0}^a x^j=\frac{x^{a+1}-1}{x-1}$:
$$(x-1)\big(x^{(a+1)b}-1\big)-(x^b-1)\big(x^{a+1}-1\big)\equiv0,$$
which expands to
$$F(x)=x^{ab+b+1}+x^{b}+x^{a+1}-x^{ab+b}-x^{a+b+1}-x\equiv0\pmod{x^c-1}.$$
Reduce every exponent mod $c$ (allowed by the remark above). The result is a polynomial of degree $<c$ divisible by $x^c-1$, so it is zero. Its coefficient at $x^j$ is (number of the exponents $ab+b+1,\ b,\ a+1$ that are $\equiv j$) minus (number of the exponents $ab+b,\ a+b+1,\ 1$ that are $\equiv j$). So these two triples of residues mod $c$ coincide as multisets. In particular
$$b\equiv ab+b,\quad b\equiv a+b+1,\quad\text{or}\quad b\equiv1\pmod c .$$
- $b\equiv1$ is impossible since $1<b<c$.
- $b\equiv a+b+1$ means $c\mid a+1$, impossible since $0<a+1<c$.
- $b\equiv ab+b$ means $c\mid ab$, so $c\mid a$ (as $\gcd(b,c)=1$), impossible since $0<a<c$.

This contradiction shows the two sets are different. ∎
